title: Sleep problems and nightmares alongside other difficulties
summary: Problems for trouble getting or staying asleep and for recurring nightmares, for any plan. Objectives follow CBT for insomnia, brief behavioral treatment for insomnia and imagery rehearsal for nightmares, with medical screening first.

problems.label: Trouble falling or staying asleep that drains the day
definitions: Takes more than 30 minutes to fall asleep, or lies awake for more than 30 minutes during the night, on 3 or more nights a week.
Spends long stretches awake in bed, worrying or watching the clock, and feels tired, irritable or unfocused the next day.
Uses naps, lie-ins or extra time in bed to catch up, which leaves sleep lighter and less regular.
longTermGoals: The client sleeps more steadily, spends less time lying awake in bed, and feels that nights support the day.

shortTermObjectives.text: For 2 weeks, fill in a sleep diary each morning (bedtime, time to fall asleep, time awake in the night, wake-up time, time out of bed, sleep quality 0-10) to set a baseline and guide the plan.

Within the first 2 weeks, and before any change to time in bed, screen for sleep problems that need medical review (for example loud snoring with pauses in breathing, restless legs, or medicines and health conditions that disturb sleep) and refer when present.
From week 3, get out of bed after about 20 minutes awake (by estimate, not by the clock), do something calm in dim light, and go back only when sleepy, on at least 5 nights a week for 4 weeks.

With a clinician trained in CBT for insomnia, set a sleep window from the diary with a fixed time out of bed, adjust it each week by about 15 minutes according to how much of the time in bed is spent asleep, and keep the rise time within 30 minutes on 6 days a week. Check with the medical team first for clients with bipolar disorder, seizures or safety-critical work.
For 4 weeks, start a 30 to 60 minute wind-down routine on most nights and move planning and worrying to a set time earlier in the day.
If in-person CBT for insomnia is not available, by week 4 agree on a guided or digital CBT for insomnia program and on how progress will be reviewed together.

problems.label: Recurring nightmares that break up sleep
definitions: Wakes from vivid, upsetting dreams on at least 1 night a week, sometimes about past events, and has trouble getting back to sleep.
Puts off going to bed, or avoids sleep, because of dread about having a nightmare.
longTermGoals: Nightmares become less frequent and less distressing, and the client feels less dread about going to sleep.

shortTermObjectives.text: For 2 weeks, record in the sleep diary how often nightmares happen, how distressing each one is (0-10) and how long it takes to get back to sleep.

Over weeks 3 to 8, choose one recurring nightmare (starting with a less distressing one), write a changed version while awake without going into trauma details, and rehearse the new version for 10 to 20 minutes a day on at least 5 days a week.
By week 4, use an agreed settling routine after waking from a nightmare (for example grounding and slow breathing) on at least half of awakenings, and note how long it takes to fall back to sleep.
If nightmares are tied to trauma memories, the clinician and client discuss by week 6 whether to offer a trauma-focused therapy alongside or after the nightmare work.

collaborativeNote: Agree on sleep goals with the client and fit every change to their work hours, caregiving, home and health. Screen for medical sleep problems before changing time in bed, and check with the medical team before sleep restriction when bipolar disorder, seizures or safety-critical work are present. Do not add names or other identifying details. Resource only. Not a substitute for clinical judgment.
